items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: But meanwhile I would take little gigs with Sun Ra... So they tried me out and so Sun Ra’d say, “Don’t play. I don’t want you to solo. Just play the notes.”

ctx.x: Okay. In 1959 and ’61, sort of surrounding, we had these records, “The Shape of Jazz to Come,” “Giant Steps,” “Kind of Blue” and then in ’61 we had “We Insist” Max Roach, and “Free Jazz” by Ornette Coleman. My question is we look at these albums now as iconic and artistic achievements, did they have any impact on your musical thinking at that time?

Oh my God yes they did. Because when I went to New York I was very regimented in a way, because I was like into bebop and playing the changes. Everything was about changes and reading. But then, being in New York, you know we had a variety of different jazz concepts. We called it jazz but the different concepts under the umbrella of jazz. And they called me to do a job with Sun Ra. You remember Sun Ra?
Yes indeed. I was going to ask about Sun Ra.

items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 17, 2022 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I got there in 1960... I went over to Sun Ra’s house... So I didn’t really eat that much because I was so excited about playing with the group that I’d never played that way before.

ctx.x: Kiwami. K-I-N-I-B-I [misspelled] Ziwati. And we were staying together in the loft on Broadway, 89 E Broadway Street. And all kinds of people would come by and sessions, and we studied, actually we were vegetarians at the time. And so he called Kiwami to come in and play for a few gigs and whatnot, and Sun Ra asked Kiwami did he know of a saxophone player. So Kiwami recommended me, because Pharoah had went with — Pharoah was doing presentations and performances with Sun Ra as well, but he had worked with Trane.…

from Alabama basically, by way of Chicago. So I didn’t really eat that much because I was so excited about playing with the group that I’d never played that way before. I’d never played that free style before you know. So when I started playing he told me to forget about changes, just think about the sound and imagery you know. Let your imagination take control.
